chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Muhammad ibn Hafs, from Abdullah ibn Talha, who said:

I asked Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) about a man who sells another man, and they are both free; this one sells this one, and that one sells that one, and they flee from a city to a city, so they sell themselves, and they flee with the wealth of the people. He (peace be upon him) said: 'Their hands are cut off because they are both thieves, stealing themselves and the wealth of the people.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on two free men selling each other and fleeing with people's wealth?
ai.summary: In this ruling from al-Kafi, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) extends the hadd punishment of amputation to free individuals who mutually sell themselves to evade debts, classifying this self-transaction as a form of theft. This highlights the Shia juristic view that 'stealing' encompasses appropriating one's own personhood for financial gain, thereby justifying the same physical penalty applied to property thieves. The scenario underscores the legal mechanism of using self-sale as a tool for debt evasion, a practice common in pre-Islamic and early Islamic societies.

en.hubeali: Ali Bin Ibrahim, from his father, from Muhammad Bin Hafs, from Abdullah Bin Talha who said,

‘I asked Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> about the man who sells the man, and they are both free. This one sells this one, and this one (sells) this one, and they both run from city to city, so they sell themselves, and they both run with the wealth of the people. So he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘Then hands of them both would be cut, because they are both thieves stealing themselves, and the wealth of the people’.
